entry.title: FreeBSD GUS Safe Memory Reclamation Scheme Analyzed
entry.content:
Links: gregoire.dev | lobsters

FreeBSD utilizes Global Unbounded Sequences (GUS), an epoch-based safe memory reclamation scheme designed to manage object liveness in lock-free data structures without bounded-epoch synchronization hurdles or expensive global scans. GUS maintains a global monotonically increasing write sequence alongside a read sequence tracking minimum observed CPU activity, leveraging atomic operations and CPU-local tracking to safely determine when retired memory can be freed.

The mechanism achieves amortization by integrating deeply with the UMA memory allocator, where bucket recycling batches polling operations across multiple objects rather than executing them individually. Apple's XNU operating system employs a similar variant utilizing a recirculation depot and deferred sequence advances, balancing performance tradeoffs such as reduced free-to-reuse latency against read-section fencing overhead compared to alternative approaches like Linux Read-Copy-Update.

entry.title: Bypassing Rust's Orphan Rule Using Generic Context Parameters
entry.content:
Links: edvong.com | lobsters

Rust's orphan rule (error E0117) prevents implementing foreign traits for foreign types to maintain ecosystem coherence. Typical workarounds, such as the NewType pattern or adding feature flags to libraries, often result in code bloat, dependency lock-in, or inflexible default behaviors.

Developers can bypass this restriction by designing traits with a generic context parameter. By using a local marker type within the trait's generic arguments, it is possible to satisfy the orphan rule and implement traits for third-party types without additional wrappers. This technique enables the creation of lightweight, independent domain models and allows for zero-cost, context-specific behavior, as seen in the implementation of the Kova ORM.

Probabilistic data structures provide approximate answers to queries about data sets while significantly reducing memory requirements compared to deterministic structures. This article explains the mechanics of Bloom filters, count-min sketches, and HyperLogLog, and introduces unsure, a Go package designed for speed and minimal dependencies.

The unsure implementation utilizes blocked Bloom filters to improve CPU cache efficiency and employs conservative updates in count-min sketches to reduce estimation errors. Benchmarks indicate that the package provides faster execution and lower memory usage than established alternatives like bits-and-blooms and BoomFilters.

This article introduces the ML (Meta Language) module system used in functional programming languages such as SML and OCaml. It explains how modules bundle functions and type definitions, use signatures as interfaces to define public APIs, and utilize abstract types to achieve encapsulation by hiding implementation details.

The discussion includes parameterized modules, which allow for modularity by accepting other modules as arguments, and the `include` directive for combining submodules. The article employs Rust-inspired pseudo-code to illustrate these concepts, making the paradigm more accessible to programmers from other backgrounds.

Ratatui maintainer Joshka has developed a new terminal protocol that draws thin border lines directly on cell edges as cell attributes rather than using traditional Unicode box-drawing characters. This approach prevents borders from consuming entire rows and columns, enabling cleaner user interfaces with space-efficient panels, tabs, and widgets.

The protocol is implemented via a patch for the Ghostty terminal emulator and demoed through Ratatui applications, supporting features like multiple line styles, rounded corners with anti-aliasing, and automated edge-conflict resolution. Joshka is currently seeking feedback from terminal and text user interface authors to refine the draft specification.

entry.title: The Need for Mobile OS Alternatives to Android and iOS
entry.content:
Links: blog.ovalerio.net | lobsters

Increasingly restrictive controls within the Android and iOS ecosystems are reducing user agency and complicating the installation of independent software. While de-googled ROMs provide some relief, trends toward centralized permissions and restricted sideloading threaten long-term digital sovereignty on mobile devices.

A viable alternative requires an open-source core, support for multiple app stores, and a focus on interoperability rather than merely copying existing ecosystems. Currently, community-driven projects such as SailfishOS, Nura, and Ubuntu Touch are the most prominent candidates for establishing a functional third ecosystem.
